ogDesc: A fort and old building from the French occupation of Chanthaburi in 1893 (R.S. 112), at the mouth of Laem Sing. Free to visit, right by the beach and sea — here's the history, how to get there, and a plan for the area.
h1:
Khuk Khi Kai & Tuek Daeng
Chanthaburi's History by the Sea
intro: At the mouth of Laem Sing, the last stop before Chanthaburi meets the sea, a small red-brick fort and an old red building stand side by side along the river. Both are traces of the time French troops moved in and occupied Chanthaburi during the 1893 crisis known in Thailand as R.S. 112 — a moment that sounds distant but feels very real when you're standing there. Entry is free and it doesn't take long, so you can easily carry on to catch the sea breeze at Laem Sing afterward.
chips: 🌊 Beside the sea at Laem Sing

blocks.html: Drive south from Chanthaburi town toward the coast for about 30 kilometers and you reach the mouth of Laem Sing, where the Chanthaburi River flows out into the Gulf of Thailand. This spot has been the town's seaward gateway since the reign of King Rama III, and it's where the French chose to base their forces when they took over Chanthaburi. What's left to see today is Khuk Khi Kai, a square red-brick fort, and Tuek Daeng (the Red Building), which the French used as their command post. The two sit only about 200 meters apart — an easy walk between them.

blocks.text: What was R.S. 112, and why did the French occupy Chanthaburi?

blocks.html: R.S. 112 corresponds to B.E. 2436, or 1893. By then France had already colonized Cambodia and was pressing its claim over the territory on the left bank of the Mekong, which led to a clash at the mouth of the Chao Phraya River. Siam had to give in to France's demands, and France asked to hold Chanthaburi as a security until Siam fulfilled the terms of the agreement in full. French troops were stationed in Chanthaburi for 11 years, from 1893 to 1904, before withdrawing under a later treaty that traded the town back to Siam.

blocks.title: Worth keeping in mind
blocks.html: The years France held Chanthaburi were years the local people lived under a foreign army on their own soil. So Khuk Khi Kai and Tuek Daeng aren't just photogenic old buildings — they're physical evidence of one of the most tense chapters in the town's history.

blocks.text: Khuk Khi Kai — a small fort with a name you won't forget

blocks.html: Khuk Khi Kai is a square red-brick fort, roughly 4.4 meters wide and 7 meters tall, with narrow slit openings running in two tiers for ventilation and to watch what's outside. The name — which translates as "chicken-dung prison" — comes from a brutal method of imprisonment: prisoners were locked on the lower floor while chickens were kept on the floor above. The divider between the two levels was an open grille, so chicken droppings fell onto the people below the whole time — a way of torturing prisoners who resisted the French. That's how the name Khuk Khi Kai stuck with the people of Chanthaburi to this day.

The Fine Arts Department restored Khuk Khi Kai in 1972 and registered it as an ancient monument. The fort still stands intact today, with information boards telling its story, and you can walk around the outside for photos. Inside is a small bare room — you only need a few minutes to see it — but standing in there and picturing what once happened gives you a different feeling than reading about it in a book.

items: What it is — a square red-brick fort, two stories tall, with rows of slit openings in the walls
Original purpose — both a gun fort guarding the river mouth and a place to hold political prisoners
Condition today — restored and open to visitors as a historical learning site
Time needed — about 15–20 minutes to walk around

blocks.text: Tuek Daeng — the French command post by the river

blocks.html: About 200 meters from Khuk Khi Kai, over toward the ferry pier, is Tuek Daeng, a single-story brick building painted red — hence the name — with arched verandas in colonial-era style. The French built it in 1893 on the site of the old Phikhat Patchamit fort, originally raised in the reign of King Rama III to defend against the Vietnamese, tearing down the old fort's bricks to construct the new building. It served as quarters for officers and the garrison guarding the mouth of Laem Sing throughout the occupation.

After the French withdrew, Tuek Daeng changed hands and was used for many things, including a library and a non-formal education center for Laem Sing district. It was restored in 1984 and now houses a small museum telling the story of R.S. 112 and life around the mouth of Laem Sing. The building sits right on the river beside the pier, where the sea breeze keeps it cool — a good spot for photos both in the morning and in softer late-day light.

blocks.title: Photo tip
blocks.html: The building's red-brick walls glow with warm tones when the sun comes in at an angle in the morning or late afternoon. Avoid midday, when the harsh light flattens the photos and the heat is too much. Come in the late afternoon and you can walk on to catch the sunset at Laem Sing beach right after.

blocks.text: How to get there, opening hours, and entry fee

blocks.html: From Chanthaburi town, take Sukhumvit Road toward Khlung district, then turn onto Highway 3149 heading to the mouth of Laem Sing. Carry on almost to the end of the road and Khuk Khi Kai will be on your right just before the Sing Amnuai ferry pier. Continue about 200 meters more and Tuek Daeng is on the left near the pier. It's around 30 kilometers from town in total — about a 35–40 minute drive.

items: Distance — about 30 km from Chanthaburi town, a 35–40 minute drive
Entry fee — free for both Khuk Khi Kai and Tuek Daeng
Parking — there's a lot out front, but it's not large; expect a wait on weekends
Getting around — driving or a motorbike is easiest; there's no public transport right to the door, so renting a vehicle in town is the way to go

blocks.html: On opening hours, let's be straight: this isn't a big museum with fixed times. Khuk Khi Kai is an open-air monument you can walk around during daylight. Tuek Daeng, on the other hand, is sometimes open and sometimes closed depending on the staff on duty. If you want to be sure of getting inside Tuek Daeng, come mid-morning to early afternoon on a weekday, or check with the TAT Chanthaburi office beforehand.

blocks.text: Where else to go around Laem Sing

blocks.html: The nice thing about Laem Sing is that one trip covers a lot — history, sea, and nature. Khuk Khi Kai and Tuek Daeng don't take long, so they pair well with the spots nearby to make the drive worth your while.

items.name: Laem Sing Beach & Ao Krathing
items.blurb: A long sandy beach by the sea, with a crouching lion-shaped rock jutting into the water that gives the cape its name. In the evening it's a favorite local sunset spot to sit and catch the breeze.

items.name: Khao Laem Sing Forest Park
items.blurb: A short hike up to views of the sea and the surrounding islands, with a nature trail. Good for anyone who likes a high vantage point.

items.name: Oasis Sea World
items.blurb: A dolphin conservation and breeding center at the mouth of Laem Sing, with a dolphin show. A solid pick for families with kids.

items.name: King Taksin's Shipyard (Samet Ngam)
items.blurb: A historical site believed to be a shipyard from King Taksin's era, on the way from town to Laem Sing — about 11 km from the town center.

blocks.text: A half-day plan for Laem Sing

blocks.label: Afternoon half-day
blocks.title: History + the sea at Laem Sing

items.activity: Leave Chanthaburi town and drive out toward Laem Sing
items.note: Stop at King Taksin's Shipyard in Samet Ngam on the way if you have time

items.activity: Walk around Khuk Khi Kai, read the history boards, photograph the red-brick fort
Walk on to Tuek Daeng by the river, see the building and the small museum
items.note: The red-brick walls look lovely in softer light

items.activity: Head to Laem Sing Beach / Ao Krathing, sit in the breeze and wait for sunset
items.note: Find some seafood around the river mouth for dinner

faq.q: Are Khuk Khi Kai and Tuek Daeng free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, both are free with no entry fee. Khuk Khi Kai is an open-air monument you can simply walk up to, and Tuek Daeng is a small museum that's open to visitors at no charge.

faq.q: Why is it called Khuk Khi Kai?
faq.a: Because of the way prisoners were held during the French occupation: they were locked on the lower floor of the fort while chickens were kept above, with an open grille between the two levels so the droppings fell onto the prisoners as a form of torture. The name Khuk Khi Kai — "chicken-dung prison" — has stuck ever since.

faq.q: When did the French occupy Chanthaburi?
faq.a: During the R.S. 112 crisis, or 1893. France held Chanthaburi as a security over a territorial dispute and stayed until 1904 — about 11 years — before withdrawing and returning the town to Siam.

faq.q: How far is Khuk Khi Kai from Chanthaburi town?
faq.a: It's at the mouth of Laem Sing, about 30 kilometers from town — a 35–40 minute drive along Sukhumvit Road toward Khlung district, then a turn onto Highway 3149.

faq.q: How long does it take to see Khuk Khi Kai and Tuek Daeng?
faq.a: The two together take about 30–45 minutes. They pair well with Laem Sing Beach, Khao Laem Sing, or Oasis Sea World to make a half-day trip around the mouth of Laem Sing.
